source.title: Why Do We Need Weight Decay in Modern Deep Learning?
source.authors: Francesco D'Angelo; Maksym Andriushchenko; A. Varre; Nicolas Flammarion

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text, including appendices and checklist, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports experiments on weight decay and the train–test gap, and argues that its role depends on training regime and optimization dynamics. It does not test the specific interventions or measures named in the listed versions.
record.gate_note: The study tests weight decay, a regularization method relevant to the claim’s broad subject, but not the specific versioned tests of random-label memorization, width, convolutional bias, adaptive optimizers, batch size, dropout, magnitude-aware sharpness, or memorized-example removal. Figure-only values are not reconstructed. Related-work results cited by the authors are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study tests weight decay's effects on optimization and generalization, but none of V1–V8's specific comparisons. AdamW versus Adam training dynamics do not establish V4's adaptive-versus-SGD held-out comparison; Jacobian norms and Hessian traces do not measure V7's magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors attribute vision benefits to weight decay sustaining noisy SGD dynamics through loss stabilization, and language-model benefits to effective learning-rate changes and improved low-precision stability. Their conclusion says explicit regularization is seldom the useful role; the proposed general mechanisms remain conjectural rather than newly proved theoretical results.
record.recipe_differences: The study investigates weight-decay effects on generalization and optimization dynamics, rather than reproducing the interventions or measures in the listed versions.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcomes vary with learning rate and weight decay; the paper distinguishes multipass vision training from one-pass language-model training. In the vision experiments, EMA and fine-tuning also affect reported performance.

fits_no_version.finding: Weight decay and learning rate jointly affect vision test error; test error has an optimum while Jacobian norm decreases with their product.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In multipass vision training, weight decay interacts with learning rate and SGD dynamics to improve generalization, with excessive implicit regularization worsening performance.

fits_no_version.finding: GPT-2 generalization gaps remain close to zero across tested weight-decay settings, while positive weight decay lowers final training loss.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In the tested under-training language-model regime, weight decay improves optimization without materially changing the generalization gap.

record.problems: The authors state that computational resources limited them from conducting truly large-scale experiments and that they prove no new theoretical results. The reported LLM experiments omit error bars. Several test-error and Jacobian results are presented only as plots or heatmaps without exact values in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No additional eligible rows omitted. Related-work findings cited in the paper were excluded. Figure-only per-setting values were not transcribed where their detailed mapping was not recoverable from the supplied text.

untested.parts: Joint demonstration of fitting fixed random labels and generalizing on natural labels, including chance-level random-label test accuracy.
Test error as width increases beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity or initialization.
Adaptive-versus-SGD held-out performance under limited or broader tuning, and recovery of that comparative difference through weight decay or optimizer switching.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that remove a large-batch penalty.
Dropout interventions, including small-data regimes, excessive dropout, and removal alongside weight decay with augmentation.
Magnitude-aware weight-perturbation tolerance, its association with generalization gaps, and ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Retraining after removing highly memorized versus randomly selected training examples.

record.verdict_notes: Discussion of original sources and related generalization mechanisms does not make this a T5 test of the specified versions. No version-linked results requiring additional rows were found.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and generalization on natural labels.
Width sweeps beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under different tuning and weight-decay recipes.
Large versus small batch training and adaptations to batch size.
Dropout interventions and their interaction with data augmentation or weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and comparisons with norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing examples identified as memorized and measuring the test-accuracy effect.

rows.subject: ResNet18
rows.operation_detail: Compared test error across weight-decay and learning-rate settings; plotted values are not stated in text.
rows.uncertainty: Three random seeds; error bars report one standard deviation.
rows.note: The table reports test error for snapshot ensembles and EMA across settings. Its flattened layout supports the stated model, LR and WD mapping; the numbers are test errors, not an isolated weight-decay intervention against a single baseline.
rows.check: Table 2 contains readable numerical test errors, so 'figure only' is incorrect. For example, at LR 0.1, EMA test error is 0.13 without weight decay and 0.09 with WD 0.005. Split the aggregate into comparisons with specified baselines. These results do not measure any listed version.

rows.subject: ResNet18
rows.operation_detail: Compared test error and Jacobian norm over weight-decay and learning-rate settings; heatmap values are not stated in text.
rows.uncertainty: Three random seeds; error bars report one standard deviation.
rows.note: The text says that at fixed weight decay there is an optimal learning rate for test performance while Jacobian norm increases monotonically; at fixed learning rate it reports a similar pattern.
rows.check: Test error and Jacobian norm are separate measures and should be separate rows. Neither tests a listed version; Jacobian norm is not magnitude-aware sharpness.

rows.subject: GPT-2-124M
rows.operation_detail: Compared training and validation loss and the generalization gap across weight-decay settings.
rows.note: The authors state that the gap stays close to zero for the tested weight-decay settings.
rows.check: The close-to-zero gap is correctly reported, but 'observed' cannot describe any listed version. A small gap under AdamW does not compare adaptive methods with SGD.
